title: Replication
subtitle: Single-leader, multi-leader, and leaderless database replication topologies, WAL shipping, and failover mechanics.
keyTakeaways: Single-Leader (Primary-Replica) replication routes all writes to the primary node and streams WAL/binlog changes to replicas.
Synchronous replication guarantees zero data loss (RPO = 0) on primary failure at the cost of higher write latency; asynchronous replication risks losing in-flight writes (RPO > 0).
Semi-synchronous replication waits for at least one in-sync standby to acknowledge WAL receipt before committing, balancing durability and latency.

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: Database engines replicate state changes using two primary log formats. Physical (block/WAL) replication ships exact byte-for-byte disk page modifications, making replicas identical clones of the primary. Logical (row-based binlog) replication streams higher-level row mutations (`INSERT`, `UPDATE` before/after images), enabling cross-version upgrades and Change Data Capture (CDC) pipelines.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: Single-Leader (Primary-Replica) replication routes all writes to the primary node and streams WAL/binlog changes to replicas.

**Problem Space & Invariants**: Synchronous replication guarantees zero data loss (RPO = 0) on primary failure at the cost of higher write latency; asynchronous replication risks losing in-flight writes (RPO > 0).
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: Distributed architectures apply specific implementation patterns and topologies for Replication:
bullets: **Synchronous / Semi-Synchronous Replication**: Guarantees zero data loss (rpo = 0) upon primary crash; strong read consistency on standby. Best suited for Payments, user accounts, and multi-AZ high-availability primaries within the same region.

**Asynchronous Replication**: Provides primary write latency is completely decoupled from replica network spikes or replica outages. Best suited for Cross-region disaster recovery replicas and read-scaling replicas.
Statement-Based Replication: Ships raw SQL strings; broken by non-deterministic functions like `NOW()` or `UUID()`.
Write-Ahead Log (Physical) Shipping: Fast and low overhead, but tightly coupled to the exact OS architecture and database major version.
Split-Brain: Two nodes both believe they are the active primary and accept conflicting writes; prevented via STONITH (fencing tokens) and consensus leases (etcd/ZooKeeper).
Multi-Leader Replication: Used in multi-region active-active setups; requires conflict resolution (Last-Write-Wins, CRDTs, or custom merge logic).

codeSnippet.title: PostgreSQL Semi-Synchronous Quorum Replication Config
codeSnippet.code:
# postgresql.conf on Primary Node
wal_level = replica
max_wal_senders = 10

# Wait for ANY 1 of the standby nodes to flush WAL to disk before ACK
synchronous_commit = on
synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (standby_az1, standby_az2)'

-- Verify replication lag across standbys:
SELECT client_addr, state, sync_state,
       pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) AS lag_bytes
FROM pg_stat_replication;

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Production deployments apply Replication across targeted operational scenarios:
bullets: **Where to Use: High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for Payments, user accounts, and multi-AZ high-availability primaries within the same region, suited for environments requiring Guarantees zero data loss (RPO = 0) upon primary crash; strong read consistency on standby.

**Where to Use: High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for Cross-region disaster recovery replicas and read-scaling replicas, where Primary write latency is completely decoupled from replica network spikes or replica outages.

**How to Use: Engineering Implementation**: When a primary node stops responding to heartbeats, an orchestrator (e.g., Patroni, Orchestrator, AWS RDS Multi-AZ) promotes a standby replica to primary. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: Improper implementation of Replication introduces operational bottlenecks and failure modes:
bullets: **Where to Avoid: Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints cannot tolerate: write latency increases by the network round-trip time (rtt) to the synchronous replica.
**Where to Avoid: Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid when operational requirements do not justify: recent committed writes may be lost if the primary crashes before shipping its wal.
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Technical guidelines and evaluation criteria for Replication:
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: Semi-synchronous replication waits for at least one in-sync standby to acknowledge WAL receipt before committing, balancing durability and latency.

**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: Recommend Semi-Synchronous replication across 3 Availability Zones (1 Primary + 2 Standbys, where at least 1 standby must ACK WAL flush) as the gold standard for production OLTP databases.
